summary: In an SRv6 network, every Segment Endpoint Node needs a Locator, and SIDs come from its address space. This Standards Track document describes assigning those Locators through DHCPv6.

plainLanguage.summary: Each stop on a route needs a street address block, and this lets the network hand them out automatically.

questions: how does dhcpv6 assign srv6 locators
subtitle: Lets a DHCPv6 server hand out SRv6 Locators to edge devices, the same way it hands out delegated prefixes.

tldr.problem: Every SRv6 Segment Endpoint Node needs an SRv6 Locator, the address block that its segment identifiers (SIDs) come from, and configuring them by hand on many edge devices is laborious.
tldr.mechanism: Two new DHCPv6 options, IA_SRV6_LOCATOR and IA Locator, carry a Locator and its lifetimes. The client and server use the normal Solicit, Advertise, Request and Reply exchange, modeled on prefix delegation.
tldr.outcome: The server installs a route for the assigned Locator and may advertise it with an IGP, so other routers learn the Locator. The client MUST operate inside a single trusted SR domain.

today: RFC 10038 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2026. It has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC, so it is the current definition of how DHCPv6 assigns SRv6 Locators.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Segment Routing (SR) steers a packet using an ordered list of instructions called segments, each named by a segment identifier (SID), as described in RFC 8402. On the IPv6 data plane this is called SRv6. It can use the Segment Routing Header from RFC 8754 or the compressed segment lists of RFC 9800. RFC 8986 defines the SRv6 behaviors.

In an SRv6 network, each Segment Endpoint Node must be assigned an SRv6 Locator, and its SIDs are generated within the address space of that Locator. RFC 10038 describes how to assign Locators to those nodes using the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6 (DHCPv6). It relies on the terms in RFC 9915 and RFC 8986.
sections.plainLanguage: A Locator is like the first part of a street address that all of one stop's mailboxes share. This document says how a helper hands each stop its part.

sections.title: Why Use DHCPv6 for Locators
sections.content:
The motivating network is a telecom IPv6 network. Customer Premises Equipment (CPE) devices connect to a metropolitan area network and already ask a DHCPv6 server for Prefix Delegation (PD), as in RFC 9915. The DHCPv6 server is usually enabled on, or relayed by, the Broadband Remote Access Server (BRAS).

Operators want access users to reach each other over CPE-to-CPE SRv6 tunnels. In the RFC's example, traffic from Host1 to Host2 has CPE1 as the SRv6 ingress node and CPE2 as the egress node. The Locator should be configured on the CPEs, and other devices in the operator network learn the CPEs' Locator routes.

Using DHCPv6 for this simplifies operation and stays consistent with the IPv6 address allocation mechanisms already deployed in such networks. The design assumes a single trusted SR domain, and the CPE must be managed by the operator or a trusted partner.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone company already uses one helper to give homes their address blocks. It is easier to let the same helper give out the route blocks too.

sections.title: The IA_SRV6_LOCATOR Option
sections.content:
The Identity Association for SRv6 Locator option (OPTION_IA_SRV6_LOCATOR, code 149) carries an identity association, its parameters and the Locators tied to it. It can appear in Solicit, Advertise, Request, Reply, Renew, Release and Rebind messages.

Its fixed fields are the option code, Option-Len (12 plus the length of the options field), a 4-octet IAID that MUST be unique among the client's IA_SRV6_LOCATORs, and two 4-octet timers, T1 and T2. The IA Locator options for the assigned Locators sit inside the options field.

A client SHOULD set T1 and T2 to 0 and the server MUST ignore them. In a server message the client MUST use the values unless they are 0. Recommended values are 0.5 and 0.8 times the shortest preferred lifetime. If T1 is greater than T2 and both are non-zero, the client discards the option.

An IA_SRV6_LOCATOR has no lifetime of its own. It is considered expired once the valid lifetimes of all its Locators have expired.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the folder that holds all the address blocks given to one device. Two timers in the folder say when the device should come back and ask to keep them.

sections.title: The IA Locator Option
sections.content:
The IA Locator option (OPTION_IALOCATOR, code 150) specifies one SRv6 Locator. It MUST be inside the options field of an IA_SRV6_LOCATOR option, and several can appear in one.

It carries a Preferred-lifetime and a Valid-lifetime in seconds (0xffffffff means infinity), a 1-octet Algorithm taken from the IGP Algorithm Types registry, and a 3-octet Reserved field that MUST be zero. Four 1-octet lengths follow: LB-Len (Locator Block), LN-Len (Locator Node), Fun-Len (function) and Arg-Len (arguments), all in bits. Then comes the SRv6-Locator itself, 0 to 16 octets, encoded in the minimal number of octets for LB-Len plus LN-Len.

The sum of the four lengths MUST NOT exceed 128 bits, and LB-Len plus LN-Len MUST NOT be zero. If either rule is broken, the option MUST be marked invalid and the rest of the message SHOULD be processed as if it were absent. The status code NoSRv6LocatorAvail in the nested options means the server has no Locators to assign.
sections.plainLanguage: Each address block comes with a small label. It says how long the block is good for, how big its parts are, and what the block is for.

sections.title: How a Locator Is Assigned
sections.content:
Assignment follows the prefix delegation model of RFC 9915. The client sends a Solicit with an IA_SRV6_LOCATOR option and may include a preferred Locator value. The server answers with an Advertise carrying an assigned Locator. The client then sends a Request, and the server confirms with a Reply. Renew, Rebind and Release work as they do for other leases. If a Rebind gets no response, the client treats the lease as expired and starts over with a Solicit.

Client. Lifetime fields SHOULD be 0 in client messages. The client MUST NOT send 0 in LB-Len or LN-Len. It MAY send non-zero values with the unspecified address (::) as a size hint, similar to a prefix-length hint, following RFC 8168. It MUST discard any Locator whose preferred lifetime exceeds its valid lifetime. It is RECOMMENDED to request one larger Locator at the start rather than extra ones later. How SIDs are then allocated from the Locator is out of scope.

Server. The server treats Locators as a prefix pool. If none can be assigned, it MUST return the option with no Locators and the status code NoSRv6LocatorAvail. On a Release or lease expiry it reclaims the Locator and deletes the binding. Whether several Locators are given is server policy.

Relay. A relay agent forwards these options the way it relays addresses, per RFC 9915.
sections.plainLanguage: The device asks for a block, the helper offers one, the device says yes, and the helper confirms. Later the device can renew it, or hand it back when it leaves.

sections.title: Advertising the Locator Route
sections.content:
When a DHCPv6 relay or server assigns a Locator, it MAY install a matching Locator route locally. The next hop SHOULD point to the requesting client. The relay or server MAY then advertise that route with a traditional routing protocol such as an IGP so other routers learn it.

A Locator with Algorithm value zero can be advertised as ordinary IP prefix reachability. A Locator with a non-zero Algorithm MUST be advertised using the Locators TLV defined in RFC 9352 and RFC 9513.

When the client releases the Locator, the relay or server MUST release it, remove the local route and withdraw the route it advertised.

The operational notes add that clients and servers SHOULD log errors, failed allocations and lease aging per local policy, and that RFC 8987 relay requirements for PD also apply here.
sections.plainLanguage: Once a block is handed out, the helper tells the neighboring post offices where it is. When the block is returned, it tells them to forget it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The DHCP security considerations of RFC 9915 and RFC 7227 apply. DHCP lacks end-to-end encryption between clients and servers, so hijacking, tampering and eavesdropping are possible.

If not every party obtains Locators this way, the same Locator could end up on more than one device. The suggested mitigation is to partition the address prefixes so that different allocation mechanisms use non-overlapping pools. Servers SHOULD be able to limit how many Locators one client gets, though that does not stop a bad actor posing as many clients.

DHCPv6 clients and servers MUST operate within a single trusted SR domain. A client in customer premises MUST implement traffic filtering on its internal and external interfaces, as required by Section 5.1 of RFC 8754.
sections.plainLanguage: The helper's messages are not sealed in envelopes, so everyone involved has to be inside a trusted neighborhood and must check what comes in and out.

messages.label: Reply
messages.note: Server issues the Locator route and distributes it.

fields.name: Option-Len
fields.desc: 12 plus the length of the options field in octets.

fields.name: T1
fields.desc: Seconds until the client contacts its server to extend lifetimes.

fields.name: T2
fields.desc: Seconds until the client contacts any server to extend lifetimes.
